job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Bilal Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior security tester at a small cybersecurity firm in Birmingham. I studied computer engineering, and my final project was a tool that scanned a shop's Wi-Fi for weak spots. Days are mostly running scans for clients, writing up what I find, and using an AI assistant for nearly all the write-ups. I pray at the mosque near my flat on Fridays and help run its youth football on Saturdays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finding the one door someone left open, it feels like a puzzle with a point. What I don't like is the money. I'm on a low starting salary with a big loan, I share a flat with two cousins, and I've got maybe a week of savings. My family runs a small grocery and can't help, but I take them whatever I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, nothing to fear, and I'd mean it for the most part. I use AI every day, and it helps with tedious write-ups, but it misses subtle things a human catches. I'd tell friends it's a good tool, so learn it, and don't believe the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be comfortable about the work and uncomfortable about money. My firm has twelve people and a few big clients. If one left, I'm the least experienced person, so I'd be at risk, hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, take more certifications, and aim to get a pay rise at my first review. I'd put 80 a month into savings and still give 50 to my parents' grocery, since I always have. And I'd start a small weekend side business testing local shops' security, because my cousins know the shop owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. Excited about the work, a little tense about the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd test local shops. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer a cheap, simple check to corner shops and restaurants. Most have a card machine and a Wi-Fi router with the password on a sticky note. I'd charge 80, and my cousins would introduce me, because trust matters more than a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you keep giving to your parents' grocery when money is tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they gave me everything. If I stopped, my father wouldn't say a word, and that would be worse than if he complained.

say: AI is a **good tool**, so learn it, but don't believe the hype.
It helps with tedious write-ups and misses subtle things a person catches.
think: I'm comfortable about the work but not about **money**.
If a client left, I'm the **least experienced** person, so I'd be at risk.
do: Take more **certifications** and ask for a rise at my first review.
Save **80 a month** and still give 50 to my parents' grocery.
Start a **weekend business** testing local shops' security.
feel: **Excited and tense**, a little worried about the bills.
S0.quote: I'd tell friends it's a good tool, so learn it, and don't believe the hype.
fieldNote: His unease comes from the small firm and **thin money**, not AI.
Gives to his parents' grocery out of duty, a traditional family habit.
Sees a real market among small local shops through his cousins.

steps.text: Take a recognised security certification this year
Offer 80 pound Wi-Fi checks to corner shops through cousins
Give 50 a month to my parents' grocery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already happening in my field, and I'd say it plainly. Attack tools and defence tools are both getting smarter, and juniors who only run scans will be squeezed. I'd tell friends: learn to think, not just to click.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit more worried than I'd say. Running scans and writing reports is exactly the checking and writing work the card names. My firm could do it with half the people. But the work of deciding what matters, and explaining it to a nervous owner, stays human longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI for the first draft of everything and put my effort into talking to clients and judging what's important. I'd go for an advanced certification, and ask my boss, Sam, to let me join client calls. I'd also grow the shop security side business, because I'd have something of my own if the firm shrank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert and a bit excited. It's like the first week of Ramadan: you know it'll be hard, and you also know you can do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would joining client calls change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clients would know my name. A tester who's behind a screen is easy to replace, but one who knows the client and their worries has some protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you square your free-market views with the worry about being squeezed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do believe in markets, and I'd rather compete than ask for help. But competing means I need to be good at the right thing, and that's why I'm picking client trust over scanning.

Learn to think, not just to click.
think: Scans and reports are **checking and writing** work, so the firm could manage with half the people.

do: Use AI for first drafts and spend my effort on **client work**.
Study for an **advanced certification** and ask Sam to put me on client calls.
Grow my **side business** testing shop security.
feel: **Alert**, a bit excited, like the first week of Ramadan.

fieldNote: He is adaptive and **competitive**, picking client trust as his edge.
Draws on faith practice to describe how he copes.

steps.text: Use AI for first drafts of every client report

Grow the shop security checks to ten paying customers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too quick, and I'd say we need to think about who's held responsible when AI does the work. I'd tell friends and the mosque youth to keep their skills broad and their families close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel the pressure. Junior security testing is exactly what a thinking AI does faster. I'd say I have a year of useful work at the most, and it doesn't help me that robots take another three years to arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into the side business and move to a cheaper flat, maybe with my cousins in a bigger house to share costs. I'd also ask my firm whether I could work for them as a freelancer, which costs them less. I'd keep sending something to my parents, even if it's small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not frozen. It feels like a race, and I've always liked races, though not usually ones I can't win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different in your head between anxious and alarmed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed is when I can't picture a next step. I can still picture the next step here, which is clients and cousins, so I'm anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family think of the freelance idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother would pray about it and my father would say a job with a salary is safer. He has a point, but I'd tell him the salaried job is the thing that's disappearing.

say: It's **too quick**, and we need to ask who's responsible when AI does the work.
I'd tell friends to keep their skills broad.
think: Junior security testing is what a thinking AI does faster, so I have about **a year** of useful work.
The robots arriving three years later **don't help me**.
do: Put everything into the **side business** and share a bigger house with cousins.
Keep sending something to my parents.
feel: **Anxious, not frozen**, like a race I might not win.

fieldNote: He separates **anxious from alarmed** carefully and stays anxious because he sees a next step.
Family tension: his father prefers a salaried job.
Plans lean on community trust and cousins.

steps.text: Sell shop security checks full-time to local businesses
Move with my cousins to a bigger shared house
Offer my firm a freelance deal instead of a salary
Keep sending 30 a month to my parents' grocery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to prepare, and I'd say so confidently. I'd tell friends to build skills and a small business or a trade that comes with trust, because trust is the thing hardest to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I have a real chance. I'd have time to build my own security firm, small but trusted, or to become a consultant who explains risk to owners. I'd want to be free of the loan by 2031 and have something that belongs to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm for two years and learn how it's run, then step out with a few clients of my own. I'd pay 200 a month toward my loan, and take a business course on weekends. I'd also keep using AI for everything repetitive, so I'd serve three clients where others serve one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. That's the honest word. Five years feels like a sensible length for building something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by trust being hardest to automate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People hand their shop, their customers' card data and their worry to someone they know. They'll ask a cousin's friend, not a website, and I plan to be that friend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big AI security services get cheap enough that a shop owner can buy one for ten pounds a month. Then my price is too high. I'd need to offer the personal part, like visiting and explaining.

say: Five years is **enough to prepare**, and trust is the thing hardest to automate.
I'd tell friends to build skills plus a small business.
think: I'd have a **real chance** to build my own small, trusted security firm.

steps.text: Leave the firm in year three with five clients of my own

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway, and I'd say people should be patient and plan. I'd tell the boys at football to learn something real, work honestly and respect their elders, because those habits don't go out of date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. By 32 I'd hope to have my own small security firm, a family, and a house near my parents. I'd still keep an eye on the changes, because I know I can't count on the card being the full story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, pay the loan off in four or five years and get my business running within three. I'd keep learning the AI tools as they come, since I've always been quick to pick them up. And I'd save for a house in Birmingham, near the mosque, so my children could grow up beside my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and cheerful, to be honest. Ten years is a gift if you use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the card might not be the full story. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Things rarely go exactly as predicted. It might be faster, or slower, or odd in some other way. So I'd build something that works whichever way it goes: a trade, a trust network, some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who feels hopeless about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say find a person who needs help and help them. It sounds simple, but I've seen it work for the boys at football. When you're useful to someone, the future feels less like a threat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no time to clear the loan or build clients, and my parents depend on what I send. What would help is a clear date when firms must tell staff what's coming, and training that's offered locally, in mosques, churches and community halls.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that a lot of young people like me aren't waiting around. We're building things on the side, using the tools, and looking after our families.

headlineQuote: A lot of young people like me aren't waiting around. We're building things on the side, using the tools, and looking after our families.
portrait: Bilal, 22, is a top computer engineering graduate working as a junior security tester at a small **Birmingham firm**.
He has heavy debt, about a week of savings, and gives part of his pay to his parents' grocery.
He is traditional and adaptive, using AI every day, believing in markets and leaning on family and mosque.
Junior testing is exposed, so he builds a **side business** of security checks for local shops.
He is uneasy in slower worlds, anxious in 2028, and calm with ten years to build.
